items.title: Human Body Systems
items.description: Eighteen quick cards on anatomy and physiology: organs, vessels, bones and the systems that keep them talking to each other.

cards.front:
**Skeletal system**

How many bones does an adult human have?
cards.back:
**206**

80 axial (skull, spine, ribcage) and 126 appendicular (limbs and girdles). A newborn has around 270; many fuse during growth.

cards.front:
**Heart**

Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta?
cards.back:
**The left ventricle**

It has the thickest wall of the four chambers because it drives blood through the whole systemic circulation.

cards.front:
**Lungs**

Where does gas exchange actually happen?
cards.back:
**In the alveoli**

Tiny air sacs, roughly 300 million per pair of lungs, wrapped in capillaries. Oxygen crosses into the blood, CO₂ crosses out.

cards.front:
**Breathing**

Which muscle does most of the work in quiet breathing?
cards.back:
**The diaphragm**

It flattens on inhalation, lowering the pressure in the chest so air flows in. The intercostals assist; they take over in respiratory distress.

**The small intestine** — mainly the jejunum.

Its villi and microvilli give a surface area of roughly 30 m². Water is reclaimed later, in the colon.

cards.front:
**Liver**

Which organ makes bile, and where is it stored?
cards.back:
**Made by the liver, stored in the gallbladder.**

Bile emulsifies fats — it does not digest them itself. The liver also handles detoxification and glucose storage.

cards.front:
**Kidneys**

What is the functional unit of the kidney?
cards.back:
**The nephron**

About one million per kidney. Each one filters, reabsorbs and secretes to turn plasma into urine.

cards.front:
**Nervous system**

What is the junction between two neurons called?
cards.back:
**A synapse**

The signal crosses as a chemical neurotransmitter, which is why some drugs act on synapses rather than on the neurons themselves.

cards.front:
**Blood**

Which cells carry oxygen, and with which protein?
cards.back:
**Red blood cells (erythrocytes), using haemoglobin.**

Each cell loses its nucleus to make room for haemoglobin; each haemoglobin carries four O₂ molecules.

cards.front:
**Pancreas**

Which two hormones regulate blood glucose?
cards.back:
**Insulin and glucagon**

Insulin lowers glucose by pushing it into cells; glucagon raises it by releasing stored glycogen from the liver.

cards.front:
**Thyroid**

Which element must the diet supply for thyroid hormones?
cards.back:
**Iodine**

T3 and T4 both contain iodine. A deficiency enlarges the gland (goitre) and slows metabolism.

cards.front:
**Skin**

What is the outermost layer of the skin called?
cards.back:
**The epidermis**

Its outer surface, the stratum corneum, is dead keratinised cells — the body's first waterproof barrier.

cards.front:
**Muscles**

Which muscle type is both involuntary and striated?
cards.back:
**Cardiac muscle**

Smooth muscle is involuntary but not striated; skeletal muscle is striated but voluntary. The heart is the exception on both counts.

cards.front:
**Joints**

What kind of joint is the knee?
cards.back:
**A hinge joint** (a synovial joint)

Flexion and extension in one plane, with cartilage, a capsule and synovial fluid between the bones.

cards.front:
**Digestion**

Where does the chemical digestion of protein begin?
cards.back:
**In the stomach**

Hydrochloric acid unfolds the proteins and pepsin starts breaking the peptide bonds. Chewing only begins the mechanical work.

cards.front:
**Circulation**

Which vessels carry blood away from the heart?
cards.back:
**Arteries**

They branch into arterioles and then capillaries. Note that the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — direction, not oxygen, defines the name.

cards.front:
**Brain**

Which part coordinates balance and movement?
cards.back:
**The cerebellum**

It compares intended movement with what the body reports, and corrects the difference. The brainstem handles the reflexes that keep you upright.

cards.front:
**Immune system**

Which organ filters ageing red blood cells out of circulation?
cards.back:
**The spleen**

It also stores platelets and helps mount a response to blood-borne pathogens. You can live without it, but you catch more infections.

items.title: Vocabulaire anglais B1
items.description: Vingt mots et expressions du niveau B1, avec traduction, exemple et les faux amis qui piègent le plus souvent.

cards.back:
**atteindre, accomplir** (un objectif, un résultat)

*She achieved everything she set out to do.*

Nom : **achievement** — une réussite.

**emprunter** (on emprunte *à* quelqu'un)

*Can I borrow your umbrella?*

Ne pas confondre avec **to lend** = prêter.

**prêter**

*He lent me his car for the weekend.*

Construction : lend **somebody something** — pas de « to » devant la personne.

**gênant, maladroit**

*There was an awkward silence after his joke.*

Pour un objet difficile à manipuler, on dit plutôt **clumsy**.

**en fait, en réalité**

*Actually, I've never been to London.*

Faux ami : « actuellement » se traduit par **currently** ou **at the moment**.

**finalement, finir par**

*The bus eventually arrived, forty minutes late.*

Faux ami : « éventuellement » se traduit par **possibly** ou **if necessary**.

**avoir les moyens de (s'offrir)**

*We can't afford a new car this year.*

S'emploie aussi au figuré : *I can't afford to miss this deadline.*

**fiable, sûr**

*A reliable source told me the shop is closing.*

Ne pas confondre avec **reliant**, qui n'existe pas en anglais courant.

**se plaindre**

*He complained about the noise all evening.*

Construction : complain **about** something, complain **to** somebody.

**améliorer, s'améliorer**

*Her English improved a lot in six months.*

Pas besoin de « get better » : *improve* fonctionne dans les deux sens.

**une échéance, une date limite**

*The deadline is Friday at noon.*

Verbes utiles : **meet** a deadline (la respecter), **miss** a deadline (la dépasser).

**attendre avec impatience**

*I'm looking forward to seeing you.*

Attention : suivi de **-ing**, jamais de l'infinitif.

**abandonner, renoncer à**

*He gave up smoking last year.*

Verbe à particule : le pronom se place au milieu — *give it up*.

**néanmoins, pourtant**

*The road was closed; nevertheless, we got there on time.*

Registre soutenu. À l'oral : **still** ou **anyway**.

**avertir, prévenir (d'un danger)**

*They warned us about the tide.*

Construction : warn **somebody about/of** something, ou warn somebody **not to** do it.

**un lieu (de spectacle, de rendez-vous)**

*The venue holds three hundred people.*

Ne pas confondre avec **a place**, plus général.

**être dérangé par ; faire attention**

*Do you mind if I open the window?* — *No, I don't mind.*

Réponse piège : « oui » signifie que ça dérange.

**plutôt, assez**

*It's rather cold in here.* / *I'd rather stay home.*

**would rather** + infinitif sans *to*.

**réussir**

*She succeeded in passing the exam.*

Faux ami : « succéder à » se dit **to succeed to** (trône, titre) — rare.

**quinze jours, deux semaines**

*We're away for a fortnight in August.*

Très courant au Royaume-Uni, inusité aux États-Unis (on dit *two weeks*).
